intro: How Finnish is pronounced and how it works: the spelling rules and a key to the symbols in the pronunciations, then the grammar basics — vowel harmony, consonant gradation, the cases, and the verbs.

sections.heading: About the pronunciations
text: Pronunciations follow standard Finnish, written as exact (bracketed) IPA. Finnish is spelled as it sounds: every letter is pronounced, doubled letters are long (ː), and the first syllable is always stressed.

Short and long vowels have the same quality; they differ only in length. The mid vowels e, ö and o are true mid vowels, lower than French é or German e, so they carry the lowering mark (e̞ ø̞ o̞). t is dental, made with the tongue against the back of the upper teeth (t̪), and n before it is dental too (n̪t̪); d, n, l and s are alveolar, as in English.

sections.heading: Symbols used in the pronunciations
sections.text: Each symbol that doesn't sound the way an English speaker might expect, with a word from the vocabulary that uses it.

items.note: pure mid e, between "ay" in "say" and "e" in "bet", without a glide
pure mid o, between "oh" and "aw", without a glide
ee said with rounded lips (French u, German ü)
a far back in the mouth, as in "father"
mid e said with rounded lips (German ö)
between v and w, with the lips barely touching
dental t: the tongue touches the back of the upper teeth, with no puff of air
n before t is dental too
always a hard g, as in "go"
the sound before it is long
not a syllable of its own — glides into the vowel next to it

sections.heading: How Finnish grammar works
text: Finnish has no articles (talo is "house", "a house" and "the house") and no grammatical gender: hän means both "he" and "she".
Instead of prepositions, Finnish adds endings to words: talo "house", talossa "in the house", talosta "out of the house". There are 15 cases, but about ten do almost all the work.
Two sound rules shape almost every ending: vowel harmony decides between a and ä (talossa but kylässä), and consonant gradation can change the stem (katu "street" but kadulla "on the street").
Word order is usually subject–verb–object, as in English, but it is freer because the endings show who does what.

sections.heading: Vowel harmony
sections.text: A word uses either back vowels or front vowels, never both (except in compounds). Endings come in two forms and follow the word: the back form after back vowels, the front form after front vowels. A word with only e and i takes the front form.

rows: talossa (in the house), kotona (at home), puhutko? (do you speak?)
kylässä (in the village), työssä (at work), syötkö? (do you eat?)

sections.heading: Consonant gradation
text: The consonants k, p and t in the last syllable often change when an ending closes the syllable — before -n, -ssa, -lla, -t and others. The dictionary form has the "strong" grade; most case forms have the "weak" one.
Many words (and most loanwords) never change, and for some word types it works in reverse, but the patterns below cover most everyday nouns.

sections.heading: The main cases
sections.text: Endings shown on talo (house). After a word with front vowels, every a becomes ä.

rows: Talo on iso. (The house is big.)
talon ovi (the house's door), talon edessä (in front of the house)
part of something; after numbers; after a negative (see below)
taloon (into the house), maahan (into the country)
table.note: In the illative, V repeats the word's last vowel: talo → taloon, katu → katuun. Three rare cases — abessive (-tta 'without'), comitative (-ne 'with') and instructive (-n 'by') — appear mostly in set phrases.

sections.heading: Where: in, at, and the direction
sections.text: The six place cases form a grid. Inner cases mean inside (a building, a city, a country); outer cases mean on a surface, at a place, or to a person.

table.note: Some places take the outer cases by habit: torilla (at the market), asemalla (at the station), Suomessa but Venäjällä (in Finland, in Russia).

sections.heading: Plural
text: The nominative plural ends in -t: talo → talot, katu → kadut.

All other plural cases put an -i- before the ending (it can change the vowel before it): taloissa (in the houses), kaduilla (on the streets). The partitive plural ends in -ja or -ia: taloja, katuja, kenkiä. The genitive plural ends in -jen or -den/-ten: talojen, katujen, naisten.

sections.heading: The partitive
sections.text: The partitive is the most-used case after the nominative. Use it:

rows: kaksi kahvia (two coffees), kolme taloa (three houses)
for an uncountable or unspecified amount
Juon kahvia. (I drink coffee.) Ostan leipää. (I'm buying some bread.)
for the object of a negative verb
Minulla ei ole autoa. (I don't have a car.)
for an action that is unfinished or ongoing
Luen kirjaa. (I'm reading a book.) — compare Luin kirjan. (I read the book [to the end].)
after verbs of feeling and some others
Rakastan sinua. (I love you.) Odotan bussia. (I'm waiting for the bus.)

sections.heading: To have
sections.text: Finnish has no verb "to have". It says "at me is": the owner in the adessive (-lla) plus on.

rows: I don't have money (partitive after the negative).

table.note: se means "it" and ne "they" (things); in everyday speech they are also used for people.

sections.heading: Possessive suffixes
sections.text: In standard Finnish, "my house" is the genitive pronoun plus a suffix on the noun — and the pronoun can be left out (except for hän and he). In everyday speech, people usually drop the suffix and keep the pronoun: mun talo.

sections.heading: The six verb types
sections.text: Verbs are grouped by the ending of their basic form. Drop the ending to find the stem for the present tense.

table.note: Type 1 verbs also show consonant gradation: ottaa (to take) → otan, but hän ottaa.
The present tense also covers the future: Tulen huomenna. (I'll come tomorrow.)

sections.heading: Negation
sections.text: Finnish negates with a negative verb, ei, which takes the person ending. The main verb stays in its bare stem.

table.note: olla: en ole, et ole, ei ole… In the past: en puhunut (I didn't speak), emme puhuneet (we didn't speak).

sections.heading: Questions
text: Yes-no questions add -ko / -kö to the first word, usually the verb, which moves to the front: Puhutko englantia? (Do you speak English?) Onko tämä sinun? (Is this yours?)
The answer repeats the verb: Puhutko suomea? — Puhun. / En puhu. (Do you speak Finnish? — I do. / I don't.)
Question words: mikä (what), kuka (who), missä (where), mistä (from where), mihin (where to), milloin (when), miksi (why), miten / kuinka (how), paljonko (how much).

sections.heading: Past tense
sections.text: The simple past adds -i- before the person ending. The vowel before it may change (puhu- + i stays puhui-, but syö- becomes söi-).

table.note: The perfect uses olla + the -nut/-nyt form, as in English: Olen käynyt Suomessa. (I have been to Finland.)

sections.heading: Spoken Finnish
text: What you hear in conversation differs from written Finnish. The most common differences:
mä, sä instead of minä, sinä; se, ne instead of hän, he.
"We" uses the passive: me mennään instead of me menemme (we go); me ollaan instead of me olemme.
Many words are shortened: mä oon (minä olen, I am), mä en tiiä (minä en tiedä, I don't know), mun (minun, my), tää (tämä, this).
